Drone, imagery and custom detection

Drone orthophotos, elevation models and volumes where the detail matters

Satellite screening covers the whole route or site. Drone surveys then capture the stretches that need a closer look, a dated cut-off record, or a measurement of earthworks and stockpiles. Drone work is carried out by Afridrone, AfriScan’s sister drone-services brand, subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires.

Used in: Oil & gas · Mining · Power & utilities · Rail & roads · Renewables

Request a proposal Imagery and data sources

What it is

Satellite first, drone for the detail

Most of a corridor or concession never needs a drone. Satellite screening maps it end to end and tells you which stretches have changed, which have the most structures, and where the imagery could not settle a question. Those are the places a drone earns its flight time.

A drone survey gives your team a dated, georeferenced orthophoto of each flagged stretch or site, detailed enough for a reviewer to check roofs, fences, gates and fresh digging, with surface and terrain elevation models, a point cloud and a 3D model processed from the same flight. Dated drone surveys are also usually the most reliable way to fix a record on a particular day, such as a resettlement cut-off date, when satellite capture dates cannot be guaranteed.

Every drone job is planned around the permits and authorisations that particular flight needs. Satellite-based work carries on while they are obtained.

Permits are part of the plan

We never assume a permit. Afridrone is working towards the operator approvals each country requires, and every drone proposal sets out the permits the flight needs and how they fit the schedule. Afridrone is AfriScan’s sister drone-services brand.

How it works

What a drone survey is used for

Checks of flagged stretches

Satellite screening narrows the search; drone flights over the flagged stretches capture the detail your team needs to decide what to do next.

Orthophotos and elevation models

A georeferenced orthophoto, surface and terrain models, a point cloud, a 3D model and a processing quality report for a site or corridor section.

Construction and earthworks

Dated flights compared side by side, with maps of where ground has been cut or filled between visits.

Stockpiles and volumes

Volumes of stockpiles, spoil heaps, borrow pits and cut-and-fill areas, calculated from the elevation models.

Vegetation height in servitudes

Where tall vegetation stands inside a power-line or pipeline servitude, from the drone elevation models, with open canopy-height data for the wider picture.

Dated records

A drone survey on a known date for a cut-off record, a handover baseline or an evidence pack.

Permits, country by country

What a drone survey needs in each country

The main requirements an operator must meet, as of 26 September 2026. This section summarises public rules for information. It is not legal advice; the sources are linked.

IACM · Lei n.º 6/2024

Mozambique

  • Drone flights are regulated by the civil aviation authority, IACM.
  • The Minister of National Defence authorises aerial surveys in national territory (Lei n.º 6/2024, de 4 de Junho, art. 13(1)).
  • Supplying the survey data to the client needs authorisation from the cartography entity (art. 13(2)).
  • Reproducing or publishing aerial photographs or orthophotos without authorisation is an infraction (art. 16(1)(c)), and so is using products of illegal origin (art. 16(1)(d)).

SACAA · Part 101

South Africa

  • Commercial drone work needs a UASOC from the South African Civil Aviation Authority and an Air Service Licence (Civil Aviation Regulations Part 101, GN R.3170, 2023).
  • Flights within 50 m of people, structures or public roads need specific approval, and the landowner’s permission is needed for each flight (SACAA Part 101 operations manual).
  • Special nature reserves and world heritage sites control their airspace up to 2,500 ft (Protected Areas Act, s47).
  • Servitude diagrams are the work of professional land surveyors (Geomatics Profession Act, s13); orthophotos do not replace them.

NCAA · Part 21

Nigeria

  • Commercial drone work needs an RPAS Operator Certificate from the NCAA, with ONSA security clearance built into the process, and each drone must be registered (Nig.CARs 2023 Part 21).
  • Standard conditions are daytime, within visual line of sight, at or below 400 ft and not over populated areas; anything else needs authorisation.
  • Controlled airspace, including around Lagos and Port Harcourt, needs air-traffic clearance (NCAA letter, June 2025).
  • Aerial photography for survey purposes needs three months’ notice to the Director of Federal Surveys, unless a shorter period is allowed (Survey Co-ordination Act, s.1).

Where a rule’s reach is unsettled, such as whether Mozambique’s Lei n.º 6/2024 applies to satellite-derived mapping or whether Nigeria’s survey notice applies to drone orthophotos, we say so in the proposal and recommend your counsel confirms it. The wider country picture is on where we work.

What you receive

Survey files your engineers and GIS team can open

  • A georeferenced orthophoto (GeoTIFF) of each surveyed stretch or site, with its flight date
  • Surface and terrain elevation models (DSM and DTM) and a point cloud (LAZ)
  • A 3D model and a processing quality report
  • Volumes, cut-and-fill maps and vegetation-height layers where scoped
  • Structure, change and corridor analysis on the orthophoto, reviewed by a person, in the same PDF and GIS formats as every other survey

Limits

What a drone survey is not

What it gives you

  • Detail on the stretches and sites that need it, on a known date
  • Elevation models, volumes and cut-and-fill for engineering and progress reporting
  • Imagery that a reviewer can use to check fences, gates and small structures

What it is not

  • Not a certified, cadastral or statutory survey: it supports your registered surveyor
  • Never a flight without permits: each job is subject to the permits and authorisations it requires
  • No thermal, LiDAR or multispectral payloads, and no long-range flights
  • Not imagery of people: flights map land and assets, and plans avoid flying over people

Frequently asked questions

Who obtains the drone permits?

Every drone proposal names the permits and authorisations that particular flight needs, who obtains them and how they fit the schedule. Afridrone is working towards the operator approvals each country requires, and no flight is planned on an assumed permit. Satellite-based work involves no drone flight and can start straight away.

Why not fly the whole route?

Because satellite screening already covers it, and a drone survey is slower, needs permits for each operation and is limited to what the pilot can see. Flying only the flagged stretches, sites or dates that need detail puts the effort where it changes a decision.

Can the orthophotos and volumes stand in for a statutory survey?

No. They are georeferenced from the drone’s own positioning, and the volumes are calculated from the elevation models. They are not certified, cadastral or statutory surveys. Where a registered surveyor is required, our data supports their work.

Can you publish or hand over the orthophotos straight away?

That depends on the country. In Mozambique, for example, supplying aerial survey data to a client and reproducing orthophotos both need their own authorisation under Lei n.º 6/2024. We build those steps into the plan.

We already fly our own drones. Can you still help?

Yes. Send your orthophotos and we run the same structure, change and corridor analysis on them. See your imagery, archive or a new capture.

Tell us which stretches or sites need a closer look.

Send the route or site, what the drone survey is for and your deadline. The proposal sets out the permits and authorisations the flight needs and how they fit the schedule.
